implementation_notes: JPA/Hibernate owns the identity field: @Id marks the attribute as the primary key, @GeneratedValue selects the generator - IDENTITY lets the database assign the key (the provider reads it back from the INSERT), SEQUENCE pre-allocates from a sequence so the key is known before the statement, TABLE uses the classic key table - and GenerationType.UUID or a UUID attribute with an application-generated value covers the 'key must exist before insert' case. The classic key-generator objects collapse into that annotation plus the provider; use plain JDBC (Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS with getGeneratedKeys()) when no ORM is wanted. Keep equals/hashCode on the id, and keep entities with an unassigned id out of hash-based collections.
pitfalls: With IDENTITY the key is null until the flush and the provider cannot batch inserts (each row needs its own generated key); with SEQUENCE the key is assigned before the insert and batching/reordering stays possible.
An entity with a null id put into a HashSet or a Map before persisting changes its hash code once the id is assigned, so it becomes unreachable in that collection.
equals/hashCode over all fields (or over a mutable business field) breaks identity-map lookups as soon as one attribute changes.

variants.name: Plain JDBC with RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS
variants.implementation_notes: Without an ORM the mapper is hand-written: prepare the INSERT with RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS, execute it, then read the database-assigned key from the returned row and set it on the object; the same value targets every later UPDATE and DELETE. The classic key-generator object is replaced by the JDBC driver plus the identity column. This is the honest choice when a project avoids an ORM or must batch inserts, where a per-row key read-back costs a round trip - in that case prefer a SEQUENCE/key-table pre-allocation or a client-side UUID so keys exist before the batch.
pitfalls: Drivers may return the full row or an empty result depending on column hints; check for an empty ResultSet instead of assuming exactly one column.
getGeneratedKeys() belongs to the statement that ran the insert - reading it through another pooled connection returns nothing.
The key is unknown while the statement runs, so a child row referencing the new parent cannot be inserted in the same batch without pre-allocated keys.

variants.name: Application-assigned UUID key
variants.implementation_notes: The application is the key generator: the field is initialised with a UUID before the INSERT, the mapper inserts that value explicitly and never reads a key back, so the identity exists before the row does - the classic strategy for object graphs, batch writes, idempotent retries and keys generated at the source. It replaces the database key generator entirely; the cost is a 128-bit key and, with random UUIDs, worse index locality, so prefer a time-ordered variant (UUIDv7/ULID) or a sequence when keys should stay compact or roughly ordered.
pitfalls: A random (v4) UUID is not time-ordered: on B-tree indexes the inserts scatter, costing page splits and cache locality - UUIDv7/ULID or a sequence keeps locality.
Storing the key as varchar(36) doubles the index size compared with a native uuid/binary(16) column, and string comparison order is not chronological.
A client-generated key is only as unique as the generator: a flawed random source or a reused value on a shared table causes silent row collisions.
